content:
The Independent Committee Inquiry into Wang Fuk Court disclosed that Wong Bik-kiu held 131 proxy votes at the owners' meeting on 11 December 2021, and 148 proxy votes at the meeting on 6 September 2024, accounting for 25% and 20% of the total proxy votes on those two dates respectively. *Sing Tao Society* obtained proxy records from four owners' meetings held in 2019, 2021 and 2024, including the list of "units authorising Wong Bik-kiu". The investigation found that at least two owners' names still appeared in the "units authorising Wong Bik-kiu" records after they had passed away; one of them died in 2014, yet the name continued to appear in the proxy records for 2021 and 2024, with one of the authorisations made out to an individual sharing the same name as a member of the Wang Fuk District Care Team. When reporters contacted the deceased owner's daughter, she said she did not know the authorised person and repeatedly stressed that her family had never participated in the estate's affairs, and that her father was hearing-impaired, saying "why would he bother with all that". Some in the legal sector are of the view that an executor or administrator of the estate has the right to vote on behalf of a deceased owner, but if the authorisation was not made by the administrator, further investigation would be needed to determine whether impersonation or forgery was involved. Reporters sent inquiries to Wong Bik-kiu via text message, email and through a district councillor's office, and also contacted the then Incorporated Owners chairman Tang Kwok-kuen; no reply was received before deadline. Related reports: Investigation into Wong Bik-kiu's proxy votes Part 1 | The network behind 131 proxy votes, 5 people suspected to be from the old Tai Wo Estate owners' corporation, embroiled in a hefty construction contract dispute that was overturned; Investigation into Wong Bik-kiu's proxy votes Part 2 | 53 individuals obtained 131 proxy votes – who are they? Some have backgrounds linked to the DAB and New Hong Kong Alliance.

A unit on the 9th floor of Wang Yan House, the owner passed away seven years ago, yet the name still appeared on the "units authorising Wong Bik-kiu" list. (File photo)

Owner passed away seven years ago, name still appears on "units authorising Wong Bik-kiu" list

After consolidating the authorisation records and land search documents, reporters found that a surnamed Wong owner of Wang Yan House (Block A) 9th floor passed away in September 2014, with her daughter obtaining the Letter of Administration later that same year, and had been handling matters as the estate administrator, though the property title transfer had not been completed.

The surnamed Wong owner's name and unit appeared on the "units authorising Wong Bik-kiu" list, showing that seven years after her death, at the December 2021 owners' meeting, authorisation was given to "Lau Wing-hung"; the agenda of that day's meeting included the selection of engineering consultant "Yick Yui", as well as a motion to replace the old owners' corporation. At the owners' meeting on 28 January 2024, where contractor "Wang Yip" was selected, the authorisation records showed the deceased surnamed Wong owner as the first owner, with her non-administrator husband as the second owner, authorising "Ng Oi-ling"; "Ng Oi-ling" shares the same name as a member of the Wang Fuk Phase 1 Care Team.

The surnamed Wong owner's daughter lives in Fu Shin Estate in the same district. She said in an interview that she did not know "Lau Wing-hung" or "Ng Oi-ling", who were authorised in 2021 and 2024.

Estate administrator unaware, father wore hearing aids in both ears

A *Sing Tao Society* reporter contacted the deceased surnamed Wong owner's daughter. She said her younger sister was the estate administrator, but their mother passed away not long before and moved overseas shortly after, while their father lived alone in the Wang Fuk Court unit. She would occasionally visit and care for him, and assisted in dealing with matters relating to the unit. As for the unit being "authorised" twice in 2021 and 2024, she said the two sisters had never paid attention to the estate's affairs and did not know the authorised persons "Lau Wing-hung" and "Ng Oi-ling".

As to whether the authorisation forms were signed by her father who lived alone, she said she was not sure, and he had also passed away in May of last year. However, she said her father had hearing difficulties and wore hearing aids in both ears, "he would not go over to listen (at meetings)", "he could not hear what others were saying anyway, why would he bother with that, he didn't like troublesome things either". She repeatedly stressed that the family had never cared about nor participated in the estate's affairs.

Another Wang Yan House high-floor owner passed away in early 2021, whose son previously told the media that his mother had handed over unsigned blank proxy forms to a familiar neighbour, and the family had no idea about the authorised person "Tam Tak-wing". (File photo)

A deceased owner's widow handed over unsigned proxy forms, suspected forged authorisation

A surnamed Wu owner of Wang Yan House (Block A) 28th floor passed away at the end of January 2021, with the estate administrator obtaining the Letter of Administration in January 2022 and completing the title transfer in June 2023. The surnamed Wu owner's name and unit also appeared on the "units authorising Wong Bik-kiu" list, showing authorisation to "Tam Tak-wing" in December 2021. The son who inherited the estate and title told HK01 that his mother had handed over unsigned blank proxy forms to a familiar neighbour before the meeting, and the family did not know the authorised person "Tam Tak-wing", suspecting that someone had forged the deceased owner's signature.

Additionally, the joint owners of a unit on the 14th floor of Wang Chi House (Block H) passed away in February and July 2024 respectively, with family members reportedly living in Sham Shui Po obtaining the Letter of Administration in May 2025; the unit also authorised "Tam Wai-man" and "Wong Hong-sang" at the September 2024 meeting, but the records did not show the owners' names. Meanwhile, a surnamed Lee owner of Wang Tao House (Block B) 6th floor passed away in March 2022, with the estate administrator obtaining the Letter of Administration in November 2023 and inheriting the title in June 2024; the surnamed Lee owner's name and unit still appeared in the authorisation records for the 28 January 2024 selection of "Wang Yip", authorising "Tang Kwok-kuen".

Regarding the authorisation situations of the two units in Wang Chi House and Wang Tao House, *Sing Tao Society* was unable to contact the new owners and estate administrators, and could not confirm whether the authorisations were made by family members; reporters also sent inquiries to former owners' corporation chairman Tang Kwok-kuen via text message, but no reply had been received at the time of writing.

Wong Bik-kiu, who was previously absent from a District Council committee meeting due to illness, was spotted by netizens "appearing" at a restaurant in Tai Po a few days later. (Online photo)

Wong Bik-kiu cited "illness" to skip meeting, no response to inquiries so far

The Tai Po District Council earlier (20th) held a Building Management Working Group meeting to discuss the Government's proposed amendments to the Building Management Ordinance, which involved matters relating to proxy votes; Wong Bik-kiu was a member of the working group, but working group chairman Lo Hiu-fung said she was unable to attend due to "illness", after which netizens discovered she had been spotted "having a meal" at a restaurant in Tai Po.

Wong Bik-kiu addressed the issue of verifying proxy voters' identities in her second affidavit, stating that many owners who returned their proxy forms were from the current term's owners' corporation committee members, community friends, friendly district councillors and fellow townspeople, or owners known to them, as well as neighbours and members she and her team had known for many years, "we have substantial awareness of their identities for the most part, and ensure owners fill in the forms and sign them themselves." Reporters sent inquiries to Wong Bik-kiu via text message, email and through a district councillor's office, asking whether she knew individuals such as Tam Kwok-wing, Lau Wing-hung and Ng Oi-ling on the "units authorising Wong Bik-kiu" list, but no reply had been received at the time of writing.

Senior Counsel Cha Sik-ngor said that if an owner has passed away, the legal executor or administrator may vote on their behalf. (Independent Media photo)

Cha Sik-ngor: Executor or administrator has the right to vote on behalf

Senior Counsel Cha Sik-ngor, who represented defendant Yau Sui-tin in the 2016翠湖花園 bid-rigging case and formerly served as a Chief Investigator of the Independent Commission Against Corruption, said that in theory, unless the owner had explicitly authorised the relevant parties to handle such matters during their lifetime and formally executed a legally valid power of attorney, the owner's proxy authorisation would become invalid the moment they passed away. For cases where the Letter of Administration has been applied for but the title transfer has not been completed, can the deceased owner's family vote on their behalf? Cha Sik-ngor believed that if the party involved is the legal executor or administrator, they may vote on behalf of the deceased owner.

Regarding cases where residents left the "authoriser" and signature sections blank when signing the proxy form, and afterwards did not know who it was authorised to, if someone filled in the authorised person's name on behalf of the owner, or even signed on their behalf, does this constitute an offence? Cha Sik-ngor said the crux lies in whether, at the time the authorised person's name was filled in, that person had already been authorised by the owner in question, and that a "false proxy" could involve the use of, or assisting in the use of, a false instrument, or conspiracy to defraud.

Numerous proxy votes appeared at multiple Wang Fuk Court owners' meetings. At the December 2021 meeting, based on the names of authorised persons on the "units authorising Wong Bik-kiu" list, Wong Bik-kiu's "friends" obtained a total of 252 proxy votes that day, nearly half of all proxy votes cast that day. (Owners' corporation website photo)

Chiu Yan-loi: Suspected forgery, recommends simultaneous "dual signing"

Chiu Yan-loi, founder of the All Hong Kong Owners Anti-Corruption and Anti-Bid-Rigging Alliance, said the suspected forgery at deceased owners' units reflects problems in the system; as the owners' corporation adopts a "system of trust", any valid proxy form successfully submitted 48 hours before the owners' meeting commences would be deemed "valid". Although it is nominally received by the owners' corporation secretary and verified by the chairman, generally estates simply place a proxy ballot box in the lobby, which is collected by the management office for checking. Legally, if the unit and owner name filled in by a "person with intent" are correct, "even if you really forge it (the signature), you cannot say the proxy is invalid"; he believes that a "person with intent" can obtain owners' names simply through land searches.

He also pointed out that there have been precedents in the past where owners' corporations received too many false proxies and therefore added reference numbers and owners' corporation chops to the proxy forms to prevent forgery, but this was ultimately overturned by the court, which ruled that under the Building Management Ordinance, proxy forms of any format are "valid". He recommended that authorisers and authorised persons sign simultaneously to prevent the forgery of proxy forms.
